newsitem.title: UK: Andersen seeks DeLorean trial in British court.
newsitem.headline: Andersen seeks DeLorean trial in British court.

text.p: The British High Court on Monday will begin hearing Arthur Andersen & Co.'s application to have reopened the government's lawsuit against the firm that dealt with the auditing activities for the bankrupt DeLorean Motor Company.
The suits were filed against the accounting firm by Britain's Department of Economic Development and the trustee for DeLorean which collapsed 17 years ago.
In 1985, the then-British government served a writ on Arthur Andersen and the hearing that began in the UK courts was taken to the Federal Court in New York which dismissed the case in February 1997.
"The firm wants the case to be brought back to London where it began instead of starting the case again in an entirely new court in America," Arthur Andersen said in a statement on Friday.

At issue in the lawsuits was whether the government agency made a new investment decision for federal securities law purposes when it agreed in 1980 to revise the terms of a put (arrangement) it held with respect to preference shares of DeLorean.

In dismissing the claim in February, U.S. District Judge Michael Mukasey said "the put revision did not cause government agencies to make a purchase or sale of a security within the meaning" of federal securities law. Since no more federal claims existed in the suits, the remaining state claims were also thrown out.
However, Judge Mukasey left open the possibility that the agency and trustee could refile their state claims in New York state court.

The suits arose out of 1978 agreement by DeLorean Motor to build sports cars in Northern Ireland. Andersen's role was to certify the company's financial statements in the agreement by the British government agency to invest 17.8 million pounds ($29.6 million) into the project and to extend 44.9 million pounds more in grants, loans and loan guarantees. But DeLorean Motor collapsed in 1981 and later sought bankruptcy-law protection.

"We want the matter to be resolved as rapidly as possible. We believe it should be tried in the UK which is its natural home and the place where it is likely to have the most rapid resolution," an Arthur Andersen spokesman said on Friday.
